notes:
I've written notes on all 34 verses. I could only check a limited number of pages, so a few things are missing:

- **Modern scholarship:** I didn't reach bibleodyssey.org or the netbible.org notes, so there's nothing from them below.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
- **Partial pages:** Only part of Enduring Word loaded (through about v. 18). Its notes on vv. 19–34 come from search previews, so they're thinner. The Matthew Henry page didn't load, so his points come from search previews too.
- **Traditions:** I mostly label a commentator's tradition only when the page itself does. Where I add a label from my own knowledge (Gill as Calvinist, Benson as Methodist, Barnes as Presbyterian), I say so.
- **No sentence-level citations:** Points marked "(fetched page)" or taken from Chrysostom come from pages I read in full that couldn't be cited line by line. The URL is given instead.

---

**v. 1**
- The journey was about 30 miles to Amphipolis, 30 more to Apollonia, then 37 more to Thessalonica. It no doubt took several days to travel almost a hundred miles (Smith). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/acts-17.html
- Enduring Word calls Thessalonica an important port, about 100 miles and a three-day walk from Philippi (fetched page). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- JFB gives the distances too, and notes that the exact site of Apollonia is not known. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_017.cfm

**v. 2**
- Whenever Paul entered a new city, his habit was to preach to the Jews first. The Greek verb is in the perfect tense, which speaks of permanence, thus this was Paul's "enduring" custom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-17-commentary
- "Reasoned" comes from the word behind our "dialogue": there was back-and-forth questioning, rooted in Scripture (Hughes, quoted by Guzik; fetched page). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/

**v. 3**
- "Explaining" literally means "opening" the Scriptures. "Proving" means "placing beside," that is, setting out evidence. Paul stressed both who Jesus is and what He did (fetched page). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/

**v. 4**
- Guzik counts the work a success, with most converts being God-fearing Greeks. He adds that the Philippian church was sending Paul money at the time (Phil 4:15–16) (fetched page). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- Matthew Henry contrasts this with Berea: at Thessalonica there were only some of them that believed (v. 4), but at Berea, where they heard with unprejudiced minds, many believed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_017.cfm

**v. 5**
- This repeats the pattern from Pisidian Antioch, Iconium and Lystra: jealousy, then a mob. Jason's house seems to have been a centre for the church (fetched page). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/

**v. 6**
- In accusing them, the mob gave an unintended compliment to the effectiveness of God's work through Paul and Silas. Guzik adds that the gospel was really turning the world *right side up* (fetched page). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- The word for the city officials ("politarchs") has been found in an inscription on an arch at Thessalonica (Vincent). https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-17-commentary

**v. 7**
- Guzik:
  - The charge was dangerous because the city feared being seen as disloyal to Rome.
  - The gospel makes Christians *better* citizens.
  - Even the mob understood that Christians called Jesus King.
  - He quotes Longenecker's suggestion that Paul may have avoided "king" and "kingdom" language in his letters for this reason.
  
  (fetched page) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/

**vv. 8–9**
- Jason paid a bond as a guarantee against further riots. Rome didn't care what people believed, but came down hard on public disorder (fetched page). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/

**v. 10**
- Paul and Silas left quickly so as not wanting to bring more persecution on the Christians there or to jeopardize Jason's security deposit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- JFB thinks further preaching would have been as useless as rash. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_017.cfm
- Henry notes that they fled the city but not the work: they went straight back into a synagogue. If others will not do their duty to us, yet we ought to do ours to them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_017.cfm

**v. 11 (the key disputed verse)**
- *Traditional reading:*
  - Guzik praises two things: an eager welcome and daily searching. When Paul preached, they had open hearts; but also clear heads. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
  - Henry says the Greek word means better bred. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_017.cfm
  - Poole says they were better in disposition rather than birth: less prejudiced, and they compared Paul with Scripture. https://studylight.org/commentaries/mpc/acts-17.html
  - Clarke thinks they were simply better educated. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/acts-17.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary draws a sermon on THE DUTY OF INDIVIDUAL RESEARCH. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-17.html
- *Evangelical/Protestant use:*
  - John Butler (on Precept Austin): Scripture was the Bereans' authority, which makes the Bible our fundamental authority. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-17-commentary
  - GotQuestions says sola scriptura (Scripture as the final authority) is clearly affirmed in verses such as Acts 17:11. https://www.gotquestions.org/sola-scriptura.html
- *Catholic view:*
  - The contrast is between actively hostile Thessalonians and Bereans who "received the word with all eagerness", not between gullible and sceptical hearers. The Bereans also accepted unwritten teachings that came with Paul's message. https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/sola-scriptura-and-the-bereans
  - Another article argues that for Paul "the scriptures" refers only to the Old Testament. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/sola-scripturas-go-to-bible-verse
  - Trent Horn suggests their nobility may have been zeal, shown in meeting during the week. https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/bible-verses-that-teach-sola-scriptura

**v. 12**
- Clarke thinks the "honourable" Greek women were probably pagans from leading families. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/acts-17.html
- Paul had nothing to fear from the Bereans' searching, because honest seekers would find his preaching true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/

**v. 13**
- This was the fifth city Paul was driven from by a mob (fetched page). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- Henry: the opponents heard quickly (for envy and jealousy bring quick intelligence). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_017.cfm

**v. 14**
- Henry thinks Paul headed toward the sea so pursuers would assume he'd gone far away, then travelled overland, which he says involved no culpable deceit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_017.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the aim was to take ship for Athens. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-17.html
- The People's New Testament says the text doesn't settle whether he went by sea or by land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pnt/acts/17.htm
- Leaving Silas and Timothy behind shows Paul had a passion for planting churches, not just making converts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/

**v. 15**
- The Pulpit Commentary and JFB both argue that Silas and Timothy did join Paul in Athens, which fits 1 Thessalonians 3. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-17.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_017.cfm
- Poole calls Athens "the eye of Greece" that still lacked saving knowledge, and adds that Satan's malice still causes the gospel to spread. https://studylight.org/commentaries/mpc/acts-17.html

**v. 16**
- The Greek word means "swamped by idols." Paul would rather have waited for his colleagues, but the idolatry pushed him to preach. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- *Patristic (Chrysostom):* the delay in Athens was providential. "Provoked" here means roused, not angry. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm

**v. 17**
- Paul's practice was to preach wherever he could get an audience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- Chrysostom takes "devout persons" to mean proselytes (Gentile converts to Judaism). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm

**v. 18**
- Guzik on the two schools: Epicureans sought a peaceful, painless life and thought the gods uninvolved with people. Stoics were pantheists (they saw god in everything) who stressed duty (fetched page). His message did not change in Athens. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- Chrysostom: the hearers took "Anastasis" (Resurrection) to be a goddess, which explains "foreign gods." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm

**vv. 19–21**
- It was the novelty of Paul's message that earned him the invitation to the Areopagus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- Chrysostom gives two readings of why they brought him there: to learn, or to overawe him at the court for murder trials. He calls Athens "a city of talkers" that still found Paul's message strange. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm

**v. 22**
- Paul didn't open with Scripture as he did with Jews; Paul began with general references to religion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- Chrysostom reads "very religious" as praise, not an insult. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm

**v. 23**
- The "unknown god" covered any god the Greeks might have neglected, and Paul set out to name Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- MacArthur identifies Epimenides—the same poet who erected the altars to the unknown god. https://www.gty.org/blogs/B190530/uncompromising-evangelism
- Chrysostom: the altar showed Paul's message wasn't "new," which answered the charge of novelty. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm

**vv. 24–25**
- God is bigger than any temple and can't be represented by anything made with hands. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- Chrysostom:
  - "God that made the world" overturned both Epicurean atoms and Stoic fire.
  - God dwells in human souls, not buildings.
  - Needing nothing while supplying everything are two marks of true deity.
  
  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm

**v. 26**
- Chrysostom: it is marvellous that God made so many from one, and keeps sustaining them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm
- Chuck Smith applies the verse personally: God sets the limits for our lives. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/17-28.html

**v. 27**
- Ellicott: "feel after" expresses strictly the act of groping in the dark. Stoics would have recognised something of their own thought here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/17-27.htm
- *A free-will emphasis (Benson, a Methodist; that label is mine):* The way is open; God is ready to be found; but he will lay no force upon any man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/17-27.htm
- MacArthur: God placed evidence of Himself all around people and within them, so that they might feel after Him. https://www.gty.org/sermons/1764/getting-to-know-the-unknown-god-part-3
- Chrysostom offers alternative readings of how God "determined" their seeking. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm

**v. 28**
- The two quotations are from Epimenides and Aratus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- JFB: the poets meant it doubtless in a pantheistic sense, but Paul used it to teach a personal God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/17-28.htm
- Poole: Paul quoted them not for authority but to shame the hearers with their own writers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/17-28.htm

**v. 29**
- Being God's offspring makes us responsible to Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- Chrysostom: here Paul was speaking to the crowd, not to the philosophers. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm

**v. 30 (traditions differ)**
- *Shared reading:*
  - Ellicott: ignorance lessened the guilt of the pagan world. https://biblehub.com/acts/17-30.htm
  - Pulpit Commentary: God made no move to punish it. https://biblehub.com/acts/17-30.htm
- *Can people obey the command to repent?*
  - Gill (a Calvinist Baptist; label mine): the command does not suppose it to be in the power of men, and the grace of true repentance is not given to everyone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/17-30.htm
  - Barnes takes the other side: it can be done. God would not command an impossibility. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/17-30.htm
  - An unnamed commentator on the same page says the command bore down the idle plea of fatality. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/17-30.htm
- *Restoration Movement (Coffman):* "repent" here stands for faith, repentance and baptism together, against salvation "by faith only." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/17-30.html
- *Reformed Baptist (Piper):* if people never hear, they won't be saved, so the verse calls for missions. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-age-of-ignorance-is-over

**v. 31**
- Paul didn't preach a "soft" gospel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- Manton (Puritan): Christ being the judge is what most shows the need for repentance. https://www.monergism.com/times-ignorance-god-overlooked-sermon-upon-acts-1730-31

**v. 32**
- Guzik answers critics who say Paul watered down his message for intellectuals: the sermon is fully biblical, and what we have is only a brief extract. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-17/
- Howson (quoted in JFB): merchants in Thessalonica and Corinth received the gospel more readily than educated Athenians, and Paul wrote no letter to Athens. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_017.cfm

**v. 33**
- Chrysostom: in Athens the opposition went no further than ridicule, and Paul still made converts. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210138.htm

**v. 34**
- Ellicott:
  - Areopagus members had held high office, so Dionysius was a man of note.
  - Tradition makes him Bishop of Athens.
  - The writings under his name are from the 4th–5th century.
  - Chrysostom's claim that Damaris was his wife is conjecture.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/17-34.htm
- Barnes: Nothing more is certainly known of this man than is here stated. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/17-34.htm
- *Orthodox:* Dionysius is honoured as a martyr and Bishop of Athens. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/1947/10/03 Damaris was the first Athenian woman to believe in Christ; the OCA says there is no solid evidence she was his wife. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2022/10/03/206394-saint-damaris-of-athens
- Erasmus questioned whether the writings attributed to Dionysius are genuine. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/mse/d/dionysius-the-areopagite.html
